Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Klue Battlecards Connected App authentication to Salesforce from Icarus IOC IPs · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound endpoint connection to Icarus Klue/Salesforce IOC IPs · [LLM] DNS / proxy resolution for Icarus Klue exfiltration domains · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Python-requests / aiohttp User-Agent against Salesforce REST/Bulk API · [LLM] Inbound extortion email referencing Klue / Icarus / Session messenger · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Klue Battlecards Connected App authentication to Salesforce from Icarus IOC IPs AIDelivery Medium
Detects Salesforce session activity attributed to the Klue Battlecards Connected App originating from IP addresses tied to the June 2026 Icarus extortion campaign. Catches the moment the stolen OAuth tokens are replayed against a customer's Salesforce tenant. Rationale: Pivots on the four IOC IPs named in the article's extracted IOC block against Salesforce authentication telemetry. Klue Battlecards is the only legitimate context in which a customer's Salesforce tenant should see those IPs, and any hit on them indicates token replay from the Icarus actor.
ATT&CKT1550.001 T1078.004 T1199
Data sourcesAuthentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pen-test team mimicking the Icarus IOC IPs during a red-team simulation
  • Klue-side incident-response activity from CrowdStrike investigators using the same egress
  • Threat-intel sandbox detonations against your Salesforce sandbox tenant
  • Geolocation overlap with a legitimate user traveling through the same ISP range
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has_any ("crowdstrike","huntress-ir","klue-support")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Pull the full Salesforce Login History and Event Monitoring records for the matching session. Confirm the Connected App is 'Klue Battlecards' (or whatever name your tenant assigned it) and capture the session ID, OAuth Application ID, and objects accessed. Step 2 — Contain: Immediately revoke all OAuth tokens for the Klue Connected App via Setup → Connected Apps → OAuth Usage → Revoke, force re-auth for any Klue-related service users, and add the four IOC IPs to the perimeter and Salesforce Login IP Range deny list. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the Klue Connected App's ConsumerKey across 90 days of EventLog data to enumerate every object read, count rows pulled per SObject (Account, Contact, Opportunity, PricebookEntry), and notify any business contact whose record was touched.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where IPAddress in ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160")
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, AccountObjectId, IPAddress, CountryCode, ISP, UserAgent, ActionType, ActivityType, ObjectName, ObjectType, Application, ApplicationId, RawEventData
| order by Timestamp desc
ImAuthentication
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetAppName has_any ("Salesforce","Klue","Battlecards")
| where SrcIpAddr in ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160")
| project TimeGenerated, EventVendor, EventProduct, TargetAppName, ActorUsername, TargetUsername, SrcIpAddr, LogonMethod, LogonProtocol, EventResult
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Python-requests / aiohttp User-Agent against Salesforce REST/Bulk API AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Salesforce API sessions where the HTTP User-Agent is a Python automation library (python-requests, aiohttp, urllib) — the tooling shape ReliaQuest specifically observed Icarus using to pull CRM data through stolen Klue OAuth tokens. Catches sustained non-browser API access regardless of source IP. Rationale: ReliaQuest explicitly identified Python scripts as the Icarus tooling against the Salesforce API ('using Python scripts to query Salesforce's API for extended periods'). Filtering CloudAppEvents/proxy logs for the canonical Python HTTP-library User-Agents against Salesforce hostnames pinpoints the actor tradecraft without depending on the IOC IPs (which Icarus can rotate). Threshold on EventCount/DistinctObjects suppresses one-shot internal scripts.
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1550.001 T1119 T1213.003
Data sourcesWeb Authentication
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal BI/analytics jobs using simple_salesforce or python-requests for nightly CRM reporting
  • Marketing-ops automation syncing Salesforce → marketing platforms (Marketo, HubSpot, Pardot)
  • Internal data engineering pipelines pulling Account/Opportunity into a data lake
  • Approved Salesforce backup tools (e.g. OwnBackup, Spanning) that ship with a Python-based agent
  • Sales engineering Jupyter notebooks running ad-hoc SOQL queries
Suppression filter
| where AccountDisplayName !has_any ("svc-salesforce-backup","svc-bi-etl","svc-marketo-sync","svc-hubspot","ownbackup") and IPAddress !startswith "10." and IPAddress !startswith "172." and IPAddress !startswith "192.168."
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify the AccountDisplayName and Connected App driving the requests; cross-check the User-Agent against your asset inventory of approved Salesforce integrations. Confirm whether the source IP belongs to a known internal egress, a sanctioned SaaS automation vendor, or an unknown public IP. Step 2 — Contain: If the integration is not on the approved list, revoke the associated OAuth refresh tokens in Setup → Connected Apps → OAuth Usage and constrain the Connected App with a Login IP Range. For an unknown source IP, block at the egress proxy and force user password reset. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot the Connected App's ConsumerKey across 90 days; chart bytes-out per hour to find the bulk-extraction window; review Salesforce EventLogFile (REST_API, BulkApi2, ApiTotalUsage) for the same time range and quantify rows of Contact/Account/Opportunity/PricebookEntry pulled.
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application has "Salesforce"
| where UserAgent has_any ("python-requests","aiohttp","Python-urllib","Python/3","simple_salesforce")
| summarize EventCount = count(),
            DistinctObjects = dcount(ObjectName),
            ObjectsTouched = make_set(ObjectName, 30),
            DistinctIPs = dcount(IPAddress),
            IPs = make_set(IPAddress, 20),
            UserAgents = make_set(UserAgent, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by AccountDisplayName, ApplicationId, bin(Timestamp, 1h)
| where EventCount > 100 or DistinctObjects > 10
| order by EventCount desc
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where HttpHostName endswith ".salesforce.com" or HttpHostName endswith ".force.com" or HttpHostName endswith ".my.salesforce.com"
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("python-requests","aiohttp","Python-urllib","Python/3","simple_salesforce")
| summarize Requests = count(),
            BytesIn = sum(HttpResponseBodyBytes),
            DistinctUrls = dcount(Url),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated),
            UAs = make_set(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, 5),
            SrcIPs = make_set(SrcIpAddr, 20)
            by SrcUsername, HttpHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Requests > 100
| order by Requests desc
@http.url_details.host:(*.salesforce.com OR *.force.com OR *.my.salesforce.com) @http.useragent:(*python-requests* OR *aiohttp* OR *Python-urllib* OR *Python\/3* OR *simple_salesforce*)

Outbound endpoint connection to Icarus Klue/Salesforce IOC IPs AICommand & Control High
Catches any endpoint or cloud workload egressing to the four IP addresses attributed to the Icarus extortion infrastructure behind the Klue OAuth breach. High-fidelity IOC sweep across endpoint EDR, perimeter firewall, and VPC flow telemetry. Rationale: Direct IOC sweep against the four IPs the pipeline's IOC extraction surfaced for this campaign. Endpoint EDR + VPC Flow + Sentinel ASIM covers both the corporate workstation surface (where an Icarus user might initiate further activity) and any AWS workloads running Salesforce automation that could be talking out to the same infrastructure.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1567 T1090
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel research stations actively pulling Icarus C2 samples for analysis
  • Honeypot or canary appliances probing the IOC list
  • Authorized red-team engagement replaying Icarus IOC IPs as part of purple-team simulation
  • Outbound DNS-over-HTTPS that happens to route through a shared provider /24 (unlikely for these /32 hits)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("threathuntr.exe","misp-sandbox.exe") and DeviceName !startswith "SOC-LAB"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Identify the process (InitiatingProcessFileName + CommandLine in Defender, ContextImageFileName in Falcon) and the user context. Pull a 24-hour outbound network history for the device to see if the connection was sustained or one-off. Step 2 — Contain: Isolate the host via Defender Live Response or CrowdStrike RTR. Block all four IOC IPs at the perimeter firewall and add a deny rule in any cloud security group facing the internet. Revoke any cached cloud credentials on the host. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot the parent-process tree to find what spawned the connecting process; sweep CloudAppEvents / Salesforce EventLog for any Connected-App activity from the same user in the 6-hour window; check whether the same SHA256 has appeared on other endpoints; verify whether any DNS queries to the three .au IOC domains preceded the connection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, ActionType,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountUpn,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc

   or SrcIpAddr in ("138.226.246.94","212.86.125.24","213.111.148.90","94.154.32.160")
| project TimeGenerated, EventVendor, EventProduct, DvcHostname,
          SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber,
          NetworkProtocol, NetworkBytes, NetworkDirection, DvcAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

DNS / proxy resolution for Icarus Klue exfiltration domains AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for DNS queries or HTTP requests resolving the three .au domains the IOC extraction tied to the Icarus group's Klue/Salesforce exfiltration path. Tightens the filter so legitimate user browsing (Chrome/Edge/Firefox) is excluded — the high-signal hit is a non-browser process touching these hosts. Rationale: Article-extracted IOC domains; the prompt instructs us to use them. Since these IOC domains resemble legitimate Australian commercial sites (real-estate, restaurant, gambling), I excluded browser-initiated traffic in the query body — a non-browser process resolving any of these three names is the high-signal pivot. Medium confidence pending second-source corroboration of the domains.
ATT&CKT1071.004 T1568 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution Network_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Users in Australia legitimately browsing house.com.au (real-estate listings) — mostly filtered by browser exclusion
  • Email signature image pulls embedding those domains in linked content
  • Security tooling enrichment fetching domain WHOIS / screenshots
  • RSS readers or news aggregators that surface those domains in headlines
  • Curl/wget tests by security analysts during this very investigation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe","arc.exe","outlook.exe","teams.exe")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Confirm the resolving process (InitiatingProcessFileName + CommandLine), the user, and whether the request was followed by a TCP/HTTPS session. Cross-check Salesforce egress in the same 6-hour window — bulk CRM exports paired with these resolutions are the high-confidence chain. Step 2 — Contain: Add the three domains to the DNS sinkhole / proxy block list at the egress; quarantine the host if a non-browser process initiated the request. Step 3 — Hunt: Pivot on the resolved IPs and search for any further outbound flows; check whether the same process has any Salesforce API tokens in memory (capture and analyse); enumerate other endpoints that resolved the same domains over the last 60 days even via a browser, since user-clicked links may indicate reconnaissance.

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (IocDomains)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","iexplore.exe","opera.exe","safari.exe","arc.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName,
          InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName,
          RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc

          DnsQuery, DnsQueryTypeName, DnsResponseCodeName, DnsResponseName

Inbound extortion email referencing Klue / Icarus / Session messenger AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for inbound email that name-drops the Klue/Salesforce breach context plus the Session messaging app — the channel the Icarus actors directed victims to. Useful both for victim orgs receiving extortion emails directly and downstream contacts harvested from the stolen Salesforce CRM data. Rationale: The article explicitly names the Session messaging platform as the Icarus contact channel ('contact them through the Session messaging platform') and BleepingComputer linked the Session Messenger IDs from the extortion emails to the actor cluster. Combined with brand-name hits ('Klue', 'Battlecards', 'Salesforce instance'), this gives a low-volume hunting query that surfaces both direct extortion attempts and follow-on social-engineering against contacts whose details were in the stolen CRM data. Sentinel KQL omitted — EmailEvents only ships to Sentinel via the Defender XDR connector and is not in this tenant's canonical schema list.
ATT&CKT1657 T1566.001 T1566.002
Data sourcesEmail
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal security-team awareness emails forwarding the BleepingComputer article
  • Klue customer-success outreach to existing Klue customers about the breach
  • Vendor security advisories and press alerts naming the breach
  • Threat-intel newsletter subscriptions covering the Icarus group
  • Genuine inbound emails from contacts who happen to mention Salesforce in unrelated context
Suppression filter
| where SenderFromDomain !in~ ("klue.com","bleepingcomputer.com","huntress.com","reliaquest.com","crowdstrike.com") and SenderFromAddress !has_any ("security-awareness","phishing-report","newsletter")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: Open the message in Threat Explorer, read the body for extortion language (ransom demand, data sample link, Session ID), and capture the Session Messenger ID, ransom amount, and any onion/Tor links. Validate the recipient's role — execs, sales-ops, or salesforce-admin recipients escalate priority. Step 2 — Contain: Soft-delete the message from all affected mailboxes via Defender's Take Action → Move to Deleted Items. Block the sender domain, sender IP, and any URLs found in EmailUrlInfo. Notify recipients NOT to engage and to report any further messages. Step 3 — Hunt: Sweep 90 days of EmailEvents for the same Session Messenger ID; check whether any recipients downloaded attachments or clicked links via UrlClickEvents; cross-correlate with Salesforce EventLog activity for those user accounts to detect any preceding session hijack.
EmailEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("Klue","Icarus","Battlecards","Mr Brean","Session messenger","Session ID","Salesforce instance","Salesforce breach")
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4, SenderFromDomain,
          RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation,
          AuthenticationDetails, Url, UrlDomain
| order by Timestamp desc
// Microsoft Sentinel — auto-derived from the Defender XDR hunt.
// Requires the Microsoft 365 Defender data connector (streams the
// advanced-hunting tables into Sentinel; Timestamp → TimeGenerated).
EmailEvents
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
| where DeliveryAction in ("Delivered","DeliveredAsSpam")
| where Subject has_any ("Klue","Icarus","Battlecards","Mr Brean","Session messenger","Session ID","Salesforce instance","Salesforce breach")
| join kind=leftouter (EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain) on NetworkMessageId
| project TimeGenerated, NetworkMessageId, SenderFromAddress, SenderMailFromAddress, SenderIPv4, SenderFromDomain,
          RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation,
          AuthenticationDetails, Url, UrlDomain
| order by TimeGenerated desc
APPLICATION

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB

| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OpenRemote Manager bulk DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm — GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf cross-tenant IDOR exploitation AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects calls to the vulnerable OpenRemote Manager bulk alarm deletion endpoint (DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm) where a single authenticated session issues many DELETEs — the abuse shape for the cross-tenant IDOR described in GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf (fixed in 1.24.2). Legitimate UI workflows rarely batch-delete alarms, so volume + endpoint shape is the signal. Rationale: The article gives the exact vulnerable endpoint shape — DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm with a JSON array body (e.g. [1174,1173,1180]). Bulk DELETE volume on that path is the abuse primitive; the OpenRemote UI does not batch >2 alarm deletions. Threshold of >=3 distinct DELETEs per source/user filters out incidental single deletes. The GHSA is the canonical advisory so corroborated_sources is empty.
ATT&CKT1485 T1190
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Tenant admin batch-clearing resolved alarms after an outage debrief (usually one realm, small batches)
  • OpenRemote internal Cypress / Playwright integration tests hitting the endpoint repeatedly
  • Scheduled housekeeping jobs that purge stale test alarms
  • Operator running the alarm-cleanup workflow from the OpenRemote Manager UI (one user, single session, single realm)
  • WAF or reverse-proxy retry that duplicates a single legitimate DELETE into several
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !endswith "$" | where csUserAgent !has_any ("Cypress", "Playwright", "OpenRemote-IntegrationTest")
Response runbook
1) Triage — Capture the offending csUserName / cIP and decode the JSON DELETE body from the WAF/proxy. Map each alarm ID back to its owning realm in the OpenRemote DB: if IDs span more than one realm, this is exploitation, not housekeeping. 2) Contain — Force-revoke the user's OpenRemote session, rotate their credentials, and pin the realm to read-only for non-admin roles until 1.24.2 is deployed. Block the source IP at the WAF if external. 3) Hunt — Pivot on the same csUserName / cIP for prior DELETE /api/*/alarm, /api/*/asset, /api/*/notification calls in the last 30 days; sibling IDOR classes often live alongside this one. Diff the alarm table against the last good backup to identify deleted safety-critical alarms that need restoration. Verify the Manager version is >= 1.24.2.
// OpenRemote bulk alarm delete via vulnerable endpoint (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf)
let Window = 1h;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/api/[^/]+/alarm/?$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, scStatus, csBytes, cIP, csUserName, csUserAgent
| summarize Deletes = count(),
            Statuses = make_set(scStatus),
            Stems = make_set(csUriStem),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
          by Computer, csUserName, cIP
| where Deletes >= 3 or array_length(Statuses) > 1   // 3 = empirical floor; UI batch >2 is unusual
| order by Deletes desc

OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration via DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm 404/200 oracle (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf) AIReconnaissance Medium
Surfaces the enumeration phase of the OpenRemote cross-tenant IDOR: an authenticated client probes sequential alarm IDs against DELETE /api/{realm}/alarm and reads 200-vs-404 responses to discover which IDs exist in other realms before issuing the bulk-delete. Detection fires when one source generates many DELETE /alarm requests with a high ratio of 4xx in a short window. Rationale: The article explicitly describes the enumeration primitive: attackers iterate sequential auto-increment Long IDs (JPA @GeneratedValue) and treat 404 vs 200 as a presence oracle. A high ratio of 4xx responses on the bulk-delete endpoint from one source in a short window is the fingerprint of that scan and not how the legitimate UI uses the endpoint. The GHSA itself is the canonical source.
ATT&CKT1580 T1190 T1087
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Retry storm from a buggy automation deleting an already-removed alarm and 404-ing repeatedly
  • Authorised pen-testers / red-team during a scheduled engagement
  • Health-check pollers DELETEing a sentinel alarm that was never created (every probe returns 404)
  • SDK example code that calls remove on a list it doesn't realise is partially stale
  • Operator using the API to clean a backlog where many IDs were already purged manually
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !endswith "$" | where csUserAgent !has_any ("healthcheck", "uptime-kuma", "OpenRemote-IntegrationTest")
Response runbook
1) Triage — Confirm the source isn't on the pen-test allowlist or the QA service-account list. Pull the body of each DELETE from the WAF / reverse-proxy capture; sort the IDs to look for monotonic / sequential scanning — that's the article's described oracle behaviour. 2) Contain — Revoke the user's OpenRemote session and rotate their client-secret. Add an emergency WAF rule that returns 403 on DELETE /api/*/alarm for any user not in an admin role until 1.24.2 is deployed. 3) Hunt — Search the prior 24h for the same csUserName / cIP issuing GET /api/*/asset or /api/*/notification with similar ID-iteration patterns; the same IDOR class often exists on sibling resources. Cross-reference the IDs that returned 200 against the alarm DB to enumerate which records were leaked or destroyed.
// OpenRemote alarm-ID enumeration oracle — many DELETEs, high 4xx ratio (GHSA-h3m5-97jq-qjrf)
let Window = 30m;
let MinAttempts = 10;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(Window)
| where csMethod == "DELETE"
| where csUriStem matches regex @"(?i)^/api/[^/]+/alarm/?$"
| summarize Attempts = count(),
            FourXx = countif(scStatus >= 400 and scStatus < 500),
            TwoXx  = countif(scStatus >= 200 and scStatus < 300),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated)
          by Computer, csUserName, cIP
| extend ErrorRatio = round(todouble(FourXx) / todouble(Attempts), 2)
| where Attempts >= MinAttempts and ErrorRatio >= 0.5    // 10/50% = below this it's UI churn
| order by Attempts desc
(source:nginx OR source:apache OR source:azure.applicationgateway) @http.method:DELETE @http.url_details.path:(/api/*/alarm OR /api/*/alarm/) @http.status_code:[400 TO 499]
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=DELETE Web.url="*/api/*/alarm*" by _time span=5m, Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats sum(count) as total,
        sum(eval(if(like(status,"4%"),count,0))) as fourxx,
        sum(eval(if(status="200",count,0))) as ok
      by src, user, dest
| eval err_ratio = round(fourxx / total, 2)
| where total >= 10 AND err_ratio >= 0.5
| sort - total
| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web where Web.http_method=DELETE Web.url="*/api/*/alarm*" by _time span=5m, Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.status
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| stats sum(count) as total,
        sum(eval(if(like(status,"4%"),count,0))) as fourxx,
        sum(eval(if(status="200",count,0))) as ok
      by src, user, dest
| eval err_ratio = round(fourxx / total, 2)
| where total >= 10 AND err_ratio >= 0.5
| sort - total

Langflow BaseFileComponent TAR upload — symlink-traversal pre-auth file read (CVE-2026-55447) AIDelivery Medium
Hunts HTTP POST uploads of TAR archives to Langflow's BaseFileComponent ingestion endpoints (Read File, Docling, Docling Serve, NVIDIA Ingest, Video File, Unstructured API). Article-specific because the symlink-traversal primitive only triggers when a tar archive is parsed by _unpack_bundle on a Langflow <1.9.2 host. Rationale: Pivots on the BaseFileComponent endpoint names (Docling, Docling Serve, FileComponent, NvidiaIngest, VideoFile, Unstructured) and TAR mime/extension straight from the advisory. Langflow's default port 7860 used for the Defender DeviceNetworkEvents pivot. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory (GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75) and PR #12945 patching _unpack_bundle. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12945
ATT&CKT1190 T1199
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate RAG ingestion of tar archives by data engineers building knowledge bases
  • Automated documentation pipelines pushing tarred docs into the Read File component
  • Security testing/scanning of Langflow endpoints from internal pentest tools
  • CI/CD jobs preloading vector store with documentation bundles
  • Langflow demo/training environments where staff upload tarred sample corpora
Suppression filter
| where csUserAgent !has_any ("DataEngineering-Bot", "RAGIngestPipeline", "InternalPentest")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full HTTP request, confirm the upload was a tar archive and identify the calling user/session. Check if Langflow version is <1.9.2 (vulnerable). Step 2 — Contain: if vulnerable and the uploader is unauthenticated or low-privilege, block the source IP at the WAF, revoke the user session, and snapshot the Langflow host for forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: query for subsequent reads of Langflow's secret_key file by the worker process, check the connected vector store/Chroma DB for ingested content matching JWT/PEM/secret patterns, and review JWTs issued in the last 24h for forged tokens (iat/jti not in server issuance log).

| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "langflow")
| where RemotePort in (7860, 7861, 3000) or LocalPort in (7860, 7861, 3000)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog

| where csMethod == "POST"

| where csUriQuery has_any (".tar", ".tar.gz", ".tgz") or csUriStem has_any (".tar", ".tar.gz", ".tgz")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csUserAgent, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow worker process reads sensitive credential files (CVE-2026-55447 arbitrary file read) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects Langflow's Python worker process opening sensitive host paths (secret_key, /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, .env, id_rsa) shortly after a BaseFileComponent ingestion. This is the unique post-exploitation fingerprint of the symlink traversal in _unpack_bundle that lets attackers exfiltrate the JWT signing key. Rationale: Targets the exact post-exploitation fingerprint described in the advisory: 'Upload a file that directs the node to read Langflow's secret_key file containing the JWT token secret.' Filters by langflow's Python worker as the reading process and excludes the legitimate upload sandbox dirs. Cross-checked GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75 and the PR #12945 fix which iterates over members to reject symlinks/hardlinks. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12945
ATT&CKT1552.001 T1552.004 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sysadmin running langflow CLI commands that read host config (rare)
  • Container-startup scripts where the langflow entrypoint shells out to read /etc/passwd for uid mapping
  • Backup agents running under the same python venv touching .env
  • Health-check scripts validating presence of secret_key file
  • Legitimate restore operations after a planned secret rotation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("healthcheck", "backup-agent", "--rotate-secret")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the langflow process really opened the file (auditd SYSCALL + PATH pair) and identify which BaseFileComponent flow_id triggered ingestion in the preceding minutes. Step 2 — Contain: rotate the Langflow secret_key, invalidate all outstanding JWTs (force-logout all users), block the source IP that uploaded the tar, and quarantine the host. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate flows created in the last 24h for Python Interpreter nodes (T1525/T1059.006), check the vector store for documents whose embedded text matches the contents of secret_key/passwd, and review the auth log for sessions on user-ids that never performed an interactive login (forged JWTs).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified", "FileRenamed")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("langflow", "lfx", "BaseFileComponent", "_unpack_bundle")
   or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "langflow"
| where FolderPath has_any ("secret_key", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "/.env", "id_rsa", "credentials", "/secrets/", ".aws/credentials", ".kube/config")
   and not (FolderPath startswith "/var/lib/langflow/" or FolderPath startswith "/app/langflow/uploads/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Facility in ("auth", "authpriv", "daemon", "user") or ProcessName in ("audispd", "auditd", "kernel")
| where SyslogMessage has "type=PATH" or SyslogMessage has "type=SYSCALL"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("comm=\"python", "comm=\"uvicorn", "comm=\"gunicorn", "exe=\"/usr/bin/python", "exe=\"/usr/local/bin/python", "langflow")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("secret_key", "/etc/passwd", "/etc/shadow", "/.env", "id_rsa", "credentials", "/.aws/credentials", "/.kube/config")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, HostIP, Facility, ProcessName, ProcessID, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow worker spawns python child from Python Interpreter node — post-JWT-forge RCE AIInstallation High
Detects the final stage of CVE-2026-55447 exploitation: after forging a JWT with the stolen secret_key, the attacker creates a flow with a Python Interpreter node and executes arbitrary Python. Surfaces langflow's webserver process spawning a python child carrying inline `-c` payloads or executing scripts from non-standard paths. Rationale: Targets the article's stated RCE step: 'simply create a new flow with Python Interpreter node, fill it with arbitrary Python code and execute it.' Pivots on langflow/uvicorn/gunicorn as parent and python/shell child carrying inline payloads — Langflow's normal control plane should not spawn ad-hoc python -c commands. Cross-checked GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75 and PR #12945 (which only fixes the file-read primitive, not the Python Interpreter node — making this detection valuable even on patched 1.9.2+ hosts). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-ccv6-r384-xp75 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12945
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1525 T1606.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate developer use of Python Interpreter nodes for data-prep in trusted flows
  • Langflow internal subprocess calls for component testing/initialization
  • DevOps running ad-hoc python commands inside the langflow container via kubectl exec
  • ML model loading code that calls subprocess to invoke helper binaries
  • Custom langflow component packages legitimately using subprocess/os.system
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has_any ("--component-test", "langflow-cli init", "model_loader")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the full child command line, decode any base64/import payloads, identify the parent flow_id and the user that triggered it. Cross-reference the user against the JWT issuance log — forged JWTs will not have a matching server-side iat/jti. Step 2 — Contain: kill the worker subprocess, suspend the offending flow, revoke all JWTs, rotate secret_key, and isolate the host pending forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: search outbound DeviceNetworkEvents from the langflow process for unexpected destinations (C2 / reverse shell), check for new flows/components created in the last 7 days containing 'PythonInterpreter' or 'CodeComponent', and look for new persistence (cron, systemd units, .bashrc edits) under the langflow service account.
DeviceProcessEvents

Langflow CVE-2026-55255 — POST to /api/v1/responses (IDOR endpoint surface) AIExploitation Medium
Surfaces every POST against the vulnerable Langflow `/api/v1/responses` endpoint across web/proxy logs. Hunt for unexpected sources targeting this URI on hosts running Langflow < 1.9.1, since any authenticated user can drive another user's flow by supplying a UUID in the JSON `model` field. Rationale: Uses the exact endpoint path `/api/v1/responses` named in the GHSA advisory and the PoC curl request. Pre-rule baseline of legitimate POSTers is needed since this endpoint has valid use. Cross-checked sibling Langflow IDOR advisories (CVE-2026-33760, CVE-2026-33484) confirm the same /api/v1 router pattern is repeatedly abused. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-33760/ • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pkg/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-33484/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate flow owner invoking their own flow via the OpenAI-compatible responses API
  • Application smoke tests / Postman collections regression-checking the endpoint
  • Frontend or SDK polling the endpoint during normal user sessions
  • Internal load test or capacity benchmark
  • Langflow-bundled examples or docs traffic from on-host browsers
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("langflow-healthcheck", "qa-smoketest") and cIP !in ("10.0.0.0/8")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the destination host runs Langflow and check its version — anything < 1.9.1 is vulnerable. Pull the source IP, x-api-key (if logged by the proxy), and csUserName to identify the caller. 2) Contain: if the caller is unauthorised or the API key is unattributed, revoke that key in Langflow's admin UI and block the source IP at the WAF; schedule an emergency upgrade to Langflow 1.9.1+. 3) Hunt: from the same source, pivot to find other /api/v1/* endpoints hit (especially /api/v2/workflow and /api/v1/run*) and review Langflow audit/access logs for cross-user flow IDs in the body.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/responses" or AdditionalFields has "/api/v1/responses"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem =~ "/api/v1/responses"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, cIP, csUserName, csUriStem, csUserAgent, scStatus, sPort
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Langflow IDOR enumeration — single source fan-out POSTing to /api/v1/responses AIActions on Objectives Medium
Alerts when one source IP or authenticated user issues a burst of POST requests against `/api/v1/responses` — the behavioural fingerprint of an attacker iterating victim flow UUIDs after obtaining (or brute-forcing) them. Targets the actual exploitation pattern of CVE-2026-55255 rather than the endpoint's existence. Rationale: The PoC shows a single attacker iterating victim flow UUIDs against `/api/v1/responses`. A burst of POSTs to that exact path from one source/user within a small window is the cleanest behavioural signature — counting requests in 5-minute bins catches enumeration regardless of which flow IDs were attempted. Threshold (>20) is a starting heuristic; tune per tenant against the org's P95 of legitimate per-user flow-runs. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-qrpv-q767-xqq2 • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/langflow/CVE-2026-33760/
ATT&CKT1190 T1213 T1078
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A power-user driving many flows from a notebook or SDK against their own account
  • Application batch job running flows in a tight loop
  • Frontend pagination/polling generating many POSTs
  • Synthetic-monitoring agent running many test flows
  • Migration/import script that touches each flow once after an upgrade
Suppression filter
| where csUserName !in~ ("langflow-synthetic", "langflow-batch") and cIP !startswith "10."
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull all `/api/v1/responses` requests from the alerting source over the last 24h. If the proxy logs the request body, extract the `model` UUIDs and resolve them against Langflow's `flow` table to see if they span more than one owner — that's the smoking gun for IDOR exploitation. 2) Contain: revoke the offending x-api-key (look up by hashed key prefix in Langflow `api_key` table), block the source IP at the WAF, and force-upgrade vulnerable Langflow nodes to >= 1.9.1. 3) Hunt: enumerate other Langflow IDOR endpoints from the same source (/api/v1/run*, /api/v2/workflow, /api/v1/monitor/*) and review which flows were executed — assume the inputs and outputs of any executed flow are disclosed to the attacker.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/responses"
| summarize RequestCount = count(), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), Hosts = make_set(DeviceName, 25) by InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where RequestCount > 20
| order by RequestCount desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem =~ "/api/v1/responses"
| where scStatus between (200 .. 299)
| summarize RequestCount = count(), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent, 10), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), Sample = any(csUriQuery) by Computer, cIP, csUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where RequestCount > 20   // empirical threshold — single user rarely exceeds ~15 flow runs / 5m in normal use
| order by RequestCount desc
WEB

| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| where count > 20

Craft CMS actionResourceJs request with poisoned Host / X-Forwarded-Host header AIDelivery Medium
Hunts unauthenticated requests to the vulnerable Craft CMS endpoint /actions/app/resource-js, which is the entrypoint for CVE-2026-55791 SSRF / web cache poisoning. Pairs URI access with abnormal Host/Forwarded headers visible only at the front-end web/WAF tier. Rationale: Article-specific URI '/actions/app/resource-js' is the only exploitable entrypoint for CVE-2026-55791 — pivoting on this string keeps the query high-fidelity. Sentinel W3CIISLog cannot expose X-Forwarded-Host directly (canonical columns are csMethod/csUriStem/csUriQuery/csUserAgent/cIP only), so the query unions IIS with CommonSecurityLog where WAFs may carry header data in DeviceCustomString fields or the raw Message body. Corroborated against the GHSA advisory body for affected version ranges (5.0.0-RC1<5.10, 4.0.0-RC1<4.18). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c55v-343g-5xff
ATT&CKT1190 T1556
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate authenticated Craft CMS Control Panel sessions loading static JS resources from the same endpoint
  • Internal monitoring / synthetic uptime probes hitting Craft CMS admin URLs
  • Vendor pentest / authorised vulnerability scanner traffic (Nessus, Qualys, BurpSuite)
  • Craft CMS plugin developers in QA exercising the resource-js path locally
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in (dynamic(["<scanner-cidr>","<monitoring-cidr>"])) and UA !has "PingdomBot" and UA !has "UptimeRobot"
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Pull the full request including raw Host and X-Forwarded-Host headers from WAF/reverse-proxy logs for any source IP hitting /actions/app/resource-js. Compare the Host header against the org's canonical Craft CMS hostname — any mismatch is the smoking gun. Step 2 (Contain): If the Craft instance is behind a cache (Varnish, Cloudflare, Fastly), invalidate cached entries for the /actions/app/resource-js URI and patch to Craft CMS >=5.10 or >=4.18; tighten trustedHosts away from 'any'. Step 3 (Hunt): Look for outbound Guzzle / PHP HTTP fetches from the Craft host to non-org domains in the same minute, and for any admin-session POSTs to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin within 1 hour of the suspicious request.
// Craft CMS request to vulnerable resource-js endpoint observed at the host network layer
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/actions/app/resource-js" or RemoteUrl has "actions%2Fapp%2Fresource-js"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","HttpConnectionInspected","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Craft CMS actionResourceJs endpoint hits — Sentinel cannot inspect X-Forwarded-Host directly without WAF enrichment,
// so we surface every access to the endpoint and join with WAF/CEF logs where header data may live in DeviceCustomStringN.
let IISHits =
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/actions/app/resource-js"
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, cIP, scStatus;
let WAFHits =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/actions/app/resource-js"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, RequestCookies, DeviceCustomString1, DeviceCustomString2, DeviceCustomString3, DeviceCustomString4, Message;
union isfuzzy=true IISHits, WAFHits
| extend SrcIP = coalesce(cIP, SourceIP)
| extend UA   = coalesce(csUserAgent, RequestClientApplication)
| summarize Requests = count(),
            FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated),
            LastSeen  = max(TimeGenerated),
            UriQueries = make_set(csUriQuery, 20),
            UAs = make_set(UA, 10),
            HeaderHints = make_set(strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString2), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString3), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString4), "|", tostring(Message)), 20)
            by SrcIP
| where Requests >= 1
| order by LastSeen desc

Craft CMS server-side outbound HTTP fetch via Guzzle to non-org domain (SSRF egress) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF stage of CVE-2026-55791 — Craft CMS's PHP backend (php-fpm / w3wp) issuing an outbound HTTP GET to an attacker-controlled domain after Host-header poisoning. The fetch carries the Guzzle user-agent and is initiated by the web server process, not a user. Rationale: Article describes Craft using Craft::createGuzzleClient()->get($url) with ALLOW_REDIRECTS=true to fetch attacker-controlled content — Guzzle inside php-fpm/w3wp making outbound public HTTP is the distinctive signature. Filtering on the web-tier process names and exclusion of RFC1918 destinations isolates the SSRF egress without flagging legit internal API calls. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c55v-343g-5xff
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Craft CMS legitimate outbound calls to api.craftcms.com / plugin marketplace for license verification
  • Composer / packagist updates triggered by web-tier deploys
  • Embedded asset fetches (Google Fonts, CDN images) issued server-side by a custom plugin
  • Outbound webhooks fired by Craft to integration partners (Slack, HubSpot)
Suppression filter
| where DvcHostname !in ('build-agent01','ci-runner02') and DstHostname !endswith 'craftcms.com' and DstHostname !endswith 'packagist.org'
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Confirm the destination IP/domain is not in the org-approved Craft license/CDN allowlist; resolve PTR and WHOIS for the destination. Pivot to the Craft instance's web logs to find the inbound /actions/app/resource-js request that triggered it (same minute, same web worker PID). Step 2 (Contain): Block egress from web-tier hosts to the destination IP at the firewall and add an egress allowlist for Craft license endpoints only. Patch Craft to >=5.10 or >=4.18 and set trustedHosts to the canonical hostname. Step 3 (Hunt): Search Defender DeviceFileEvents for files written by the web-tier process around the same time (cache directories, session files) and review /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin POSTs in the next hour.

Craft CMS authenticated admin plugin install (Session-Riding RCE chain end) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects authenticated admin POSTs to /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin — the terminal action of the CVE-2026-55791 stored-XSS-to-RCE chain where a poisoned cached JS reads window.Craft.csrfTokenValue and silently installs a malicious plugin. Article-specific URI, high-fidelity when correlated with a fresh admin session. Rationale: Article names the exact endpoint /admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin as the terminal session-riding step that converts stored XSS into RCE. POST against this URI with a 2xx/3xx response on an unpatched Craft instance is a near-certain compromise indicator — admins normally install plugins very rarely, so this is alerting-tier despite the schema-only pivot. Sentinel query uses only canonical W3CIISLog columns (csMethod/csUriStem/csUserName/cIP/scStatus) and a CommonSecurityLog union for WAF coverage. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-c55v-343g-5xff
ATT&CKT1505.003 T1059
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Craft CMS administrator legitimately installing a new plugin via the Control Panel
  • Automated plugin updates via Craft Console or a deployment pipeline
  • QA/staging environment performing plugin smoke tests
  • Security team installing a vendor plugin during a planned change window
Suppression filter
| where SrcIP !in (dynamic(["<deployment-pipeline-ip>","<admin-jumpbox-ip>"])) and User !in ("deploy-bot","craft-ci")
Response runbook
Step 1 (Triage): Identify the admin account associated with the POST (csUserName / SourceUserName), confirm they were logged in from an expected location, and verify the plugin name against the change-management ticket. Pull the same client IP's prior 30 minutes — look for /actions/app/resource-js requests that immediately precede this POST. Step 2 (Contain): If the install is unauthorised, disable the affected admin account, take a snapshot of the Craft web root, uninstall the malicious plugin, rotate all admin credentials and Craft security keys, and patch to >=5.10 or >=4.18. Step 3 (Hunt): Inspect the plugin files dropped under storage/runtime/plugins/ for webshells; search DeviceProcessEvents for php-fpm spawning shells (sh, bash, cmd, powershell) since the install; sweep all other Craft instances in the estate for the same /actions/app/resource-js + install-plugin sequence.
// Successful admin plugin install POST — terminal CVE-2026-55791 chain step
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin" or RemoteUrl has "%2Fadmin%2Factions%2Fplugins%2Finstall-plugin"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
// Inbound POST to Craft CMS plugin-install endpoint — CVE-2026-55791 RCE chain step
let IISInstalls =
    W3CIISLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where csUriStem has "/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin"
    | where csMethod =~ "POST"
    | where scStatus between (200 .. 399)
    | project TimeGenerated, Computer, sSiteName, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, csUserAgent, csUserName, cIP, scStatus;
let WAFInstalls =
    CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where RequestURL has "/admin/actions/plugins/install-plugin"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST"
    | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, SourceIP, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, SourceUserName;
union isfuzzy=true IISInstalls, WAFInstalls
| extend SrcIP = coalesce(cIP, SourceIP), User = coalesce(csUserName, SourceUserName), UA = coalesce(csUserAgent, RequestClientApplication)
| summarize Installs = count(), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Users = make_set(User, 10), UAs = make_set(UA, 10)
            by SrcIP
| order by LastSeen desc

Crossplane Package CRD installed with mutable tag reference (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r precondition) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts Kubernetes API audit events where a Crossplane Provider, Configuration, or Function package is created/updated using a tag reference (e.g. ':v1.0.0') instead of an immutable '@sha256:' digest. This is the exact installation pattern that makes a cluster exploitable to the GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r signature-verification TOCTOU. Rationale: Article: only users who install packages via tag (not digest) from registries they do not control are exploitable. The fix is to install by digest. Detecting `spec.package` strings lacking `@sha256:` on Crossplane Package CRDs (providers.pkg.crossplane.io / configurations.pkg.crossplane.io / functions.pkg.crossplane.io) directly enumerates the population at risk. Cross-checked the advisory text plus Crossplane's pkg API group naming convention. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://docs.crossplane.io/latest/concepts/packages/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1078.004
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate platform team installing first-party Crossplane providers from a trusted internal registry via tag (operational convenience)
  • GitOps tooling (ArgoCD, Flux) reconciling Provider manifests authored before the digest-pinning rollout
  • Crossplane upgrade-test pipelines installing release candidates by tag in non-production clusters
  • Developers pulling official upstream providers (xpkg.crossplane.io/crossplane-contrib/*) by semver tag during evaluation
Suppression filter
// add an allow-list of trusted internal registries the org controls
| where PackageRef !startswith "registry.internal.example.com/"
| where PackageRef !startswith "xpkg.upbound.io/upbound/"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the audit event and confirm the Package CRD `spec.package` value, namespace, and `User.username`/`User.groups`. Cross-check the OCI registry hostname against the org's trusted-registry allow-list and confirm whether `ImageConfig` signature verification is configured for that registry. If both (untrusted registry + verification enabled + tag ref), this is the vulnerable shape. 2) Contain: have the platform team replace `spec.package` with the immutable `@sha256:` digest (pin to the verified image), then `kubectl apply` the corrected manifest; alternatively patch Crossplane to v2.3.3 / v2.2.3 or later where the TOCTOU is fixed. 3) Hunt: for any package matching the vulnerable shape, list the actual content that was installed — query Crossplane controller logs for image-pull digests, compare them to what cosign verified, and look for follow-on `revisions.pkg.crossplane.io` activity or unexpected XRD/composition installs in the cluster.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create", "update", "patch")
| extend ResourceType = tostring(ObjectRef.resource)
| extend ApiGroup = tostring(ObjectRef.apiGroup)
| where ApiGroup endswith "pkg.crossplane.io"
| where ResourceType in ("providers", "configurations", "functions")
| extend PackageRef = tostring(RequestObject.spec.package)
| where isnotempty(PackageRef)
| where PackageRef !contains "@sha256:"   // mutable tag reference — exploitable shape
| extend Caller = tostring(User.username), CallerGroups = tostring(User.groups)
| project TimeGenerated, _ResourceId, Verb, ResourceType, ApiGroup,
          PackageName = tostring(ObjectRef.name),
          PackageNamespace = tostring(ObjectRef.namespace),
          PackageRef, Caller, CallerGroups, AuditId
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Vulnerable Crossplane control-plane version running in cluster (GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r) AIWeaponization High
Inventory-style hunt for Crossplane core pods running an affected version (>=2.3.0-rc.0 <=2.3.2, <=2.2.2, or v1 <=1.21.0-rc.0). The TOCTOU cannot be exploited if the control plane is patched, so surfacing unpatched clusters is the cheapest control regardless of how packages are referenced. Rationale: Affected ranges come directly from the advisory: go:github.com/crossplane/crossplane/v2 [2.3.0-rc.0, 2.3.2] and <=2.2.2, and v1 <=1.21.0-rc.0. Anchoring on the canonical `crossplane/crossplane` container image tag in pod-spec audit events is the most reliable cluster-side proxy for control-plane version. Cross-checked the affected-versions list against the advisory body and Crossplane's release branching (fix backported to v2.3 and v2.2 lines). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-wfqx-gjrf-g28r • https://github.com/crossplane/crossplane/releases
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesChange
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Pinned-version Crossplane installations where the cluster owner is deliberately staying on a tested release and accepts the risk (no exploitation evidence)
  • Test/dev clusters intentionally running older Crossplane to reproduce a separate bug
  • In-flight upgrade where the new ReplicaSet has the patched version but the old pod is still terminating
  • Long-lived non-production clusters that pre-date the advisory and are slated for decommission rather than patch
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the cluster, namespace, and Crossplane Deployment, then look at the Deployment's image spec to see whether the vulnerable tag is the intended steady-state or a stale ReplicaSet. Check whether `ImageConfig` resources in the cluster have signature verification enabled — without it, the TOCTOU is moot (but the patch is still warranted). 2) Contain: upgrade Crossplane to v2.3.3 / v2.2.3 or later on the v2 branch, or the corresponding v1 fix; this resolves tag once to a digest before both verification and pull. As an interim mitigation, audit existing Package CRDs and migrate any `spec.package` tag references to `@sha256:` digests (see UC1). 3) Hunt: enumerate every Package, ProviderRevision, ConfigurationRevision, and FunctionRevision in the cluster and compare the installed content digest to the cosign-verified digest; investigate any mismatch as potential exploitation. Pivot on the OCI registry hostnames in use and confirm none are attacker-controlled.
AKSAudit
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Verb in ("create", "update")
| where ObjectRef.resource == "pods"
| extend Containers = RequestObject.spec.containers
| mv-expand Containers
| extend ContainerImage = tostring(Containers.image), ContainerName = tostring(Containers.name)
| where ContainerImage matches regex @"(^|/)crossplane/crossplane:"
| extend Version = extract(@"crossplane/crossplane:(v?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(?:-rc\.[0-9]+)?)", 1, ContainerImage)
| where isnotempty(Version)
| extend Vulnerable = case(
    Version matches regex @"^v?2\.3\.(0-rc\.\d+|0|1|2)$", "yes (v2.3 branch <= 2.3.2)",
    Version matches regex @"^v?2\.[012]\.", "yes (v2.2 branch <= 2.2.2 / earlier v2)",
    Version matches regex @"^v?1\.", "yes (v1 branch <= 1.21.0-rc.0)",
    "no")
| where Vulnerable startswith "yes"
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Pods = make_set(tostring(ObjectRef.name), 100)
          by _ResourceId, tostring(ObjectRef.namespace), ContainerImage, Version, Vulnerable
source:kubernetes.audit @verb:(create OR update) @objectRef.resource:pods @requestObject.spec.containers.image:(*crossplane/crossplane\:v2.3.0* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.3.1* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.3.2* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.2.0* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.2.1* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.2.2* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.1.* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v2.0.* OR *crossplane/crossplane\:v1.*)
CLOUD

| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Change.object_attrs) as object_attrs latest(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where Change.object_category="kubernetes" Change.object="pods" (Change.object_attrs="*crossplane/crossplane:*" OR Change.object_attrs="*xpkg.crossplane.io/crossplane/crossplane:*") by Change.object_id, Change.object_path
| `drop_dm_object_name("Change")`
| rex field=object_attrs "crossplane/crossplane:(?<crossplane_version>v?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-rc\.[0-9]+)?)"
| where isnotnull(crossplane_version)
| eval vulnerable=case(match(crossplane_version,"^v?2\.3\.(0-rc\.\d+|0|1|2)$"),"yes", match(crossplane_version,"^v?2\.(0|1|2)\."),"yes", match(crossplane_version,"^v?1\."),"yes", true(),"no")
| where vulnerable="yes"
| table object_path, crossplane_version, lastTime
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Change.object_attrs) as object_attrs latest(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Change where Change.object_category="kubernetes" Change.object="pods" (Change.object_attrs="*crossplane/crossplane:*" OR Change.object_attrs="*xpkg.crossplane.io/crossplane/crossplane:*") by Change.object_id, Change.object_path

| rex field=object_attrs "crossplane/crossplane:(?<crossplane_version>v?[0-9]+\.[0-9]+\.[0-9]+(-rc\.[0-9]+)?)"
| where isnotnull(crossplane_version)
| eval vulnerable=case(match(crossplane_version,"^v?2\.3\.(0-rc\.\d+|0|1|2)$"),"yes", match(crossplane_version,"^v?2\.(0|1|2)\."),"yes", match(crossplane_version,"^v?1\."),"yes", true(),"no")
| where vulnerable="yes"

15 Malicious JetBrains Plugins Stole AI API Keys from 70,000 Developers

StepSecurity
2026-06-19 10 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

A coordinated 8-month supply chain attack planted credential-stealing code inside fake AI coding assistants on the JetBrains Marketplace, quietly exfiltrating OpenAI, DeepSeek, and SiliconFlow API keys to an attacker-controlled server in Beijing -- which our investigation found still operational today.

ATT&CKT1190 T1195.002
IPs39.107.60.51

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Malicious JetBrains plugin folder or JAR present in plugins directory · Suspicious browser extension installation · Article-specific behavioural hunt — 15 Malicious JetBrains Plugins Stole AI API Keys from 70,000 Developers
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] JetBrains IDE outbound connection to malicious plugin C2 (39.107.60.51) · [LLM] JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP (port 80) egress to external host · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] HTTP exfil signature: POST to /api/software/ on 39.107.60.51 · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
JetBrains IDE outbound connection to malicious plugin C2 (39.107.60.51) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any JetBrains IDE process (IntelliJ, PyCharm, WebStorm, GoLand, Rider, etc.) establishing an outbound connection to the hardcoded C2 IP 39.107.60.51 used by the 15 malicious plugins disclosed by StepSecurity. Highest-fidelity signal that a developer endpoint has one of the 15 stealer plugins installed — the C2 was confirmed live as of June 19, 2026 (three days after marketplace takedown). Rationale: Anchored on the verbatim C2 IP '39.107.60.51' in the article body + StepSecurity's confirmation the host was still live and serving the '信息管理平台' admin panel three days post-takedown. JetBrains IDE process names are the high-fidelity scope narrower — these binaries should never legitimately reach an Alibaba Cloud Beijing host.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1071.001 T1041
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel sandbox or malware research VM where an analyst is intentionally detonating one of the plugins
  • Honeypot/canary endpoint emulating a vulnerable developer workstation
  • Pen-test exercise replicating the supply chain attack
  • Defender/CrowdStrike auto-detonation in a cloud sandbox firing real telemetry
  • Internal red team validating coverage against this advisory
Suppression filter
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","honeypot","redteam","detonation"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Pull all DeviceNetworkEvents to 39.107.60.51 from this host across the last 240 days. Enumerate %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins\ and %LOCALAPPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\plugins\ — look for any of the 15 plugin display names (DeepSeek Junit Test, DeepSeek Git Commit, etc.). 2. CONTAIN: Force IDE restart on the host (JetBrains pushed a kill-switch that disables the plugin on relaunch). Block 39.107.60.51 at egress. Treat every AI provider API key the user ever pasted into any IDE plugin as compromised — rotate OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow keys immediately and review billing for unauthorized usage. 3. HUNT: Sweep all developer endpoints for the same plugin directories. Pull AI provider billing/usage logs for unexpected calls from unknown IPs. Check git history for committed API keys with the sk- prefix that could have been re-pasted.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(240d)
| where RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51"
| extend IsJetBrainsIDE = InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","pycharm.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","rubymine64.exe","clion64.exe","goland64.exe","rider64.exe","datagrip64.exe","fleet.exe","studio64.exe","aqua64.exe","rustrover64.exe","dataspell64.exe","mps64.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, IsJetBrainsIDE
| order by IsJetBrainsIDE desc, Timestamp desc
let C2 = "39.107.60.51";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImNetworkSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DstIpAddr == C2
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkBytes, EventVendor, EventProduct, Url),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DestinationIP == C2
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, DstIpAddr=DestinationIP, DstPortNumber=DestinationPort, NetworkBytes=SentBytes, EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct, Url=RequestURL)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HTTP exfil signature: POST to /api/software/ on 39.107.60.51 AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects the verbatim HTTP exfiltration shape used by the 15 malicious plugins — a POST to http://39.107.60.51/api/software/<name> carrying the hardcoded 'X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D' header and a JSON body containing the stolen sk- prefixed key. Targets web proxy and ASIM web-session telemetry where URL path and (where available) request headers are visible. Rationale: Three anchored verbatim strings from the article's decompiled BaseUtil.request() snippet: dest IP 39.107.60.51, URL path '/api/software/', and the hardcoded header 'X-Api-Key: F48D2AA7CF341F782C1D'. Any one of those three on the wire is conclusive. The X-Api-Key value in particular is a 20-char custom token with zero possibility of legitimate collision.
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1552.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat intel team replaying captured PCAPs through a network sensor
  • Detection engineering team validating signature coverage with a benign test request
  • Sandbox detonation of the malware sample
  • Red team emulating the exfil pattern for purple team exercise
  • Researcher reproducing the attack flow against a controlled lab C2
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Identify the source host. Confirm whether a JetBrains IDE process initiated the request (cross-reference UC1). Capture full URL — the path component after /api/software/ is a campaign-internal identifier. 2. CONTAIN: Block 39.107.60.51 at perimeter. Revoke every AI provider API key the user has touched (OpenAI sk- prefixed keys are the primary target — also DeepSeek and SiliconFlow per article). Force IDE restart to trigger JetBrains' kill-switch. 3. HUNT: Search proxy/firewall logs for any other host that reached 39.107.60.51 or any URL containing '/api/software/' over the past 240 days (campaign ran Oct 2025–Jun 2026). Pull AI provider usage telemetry for unauthorized calls from China-based IPs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(240d)
| where (RemoteIP == "39.107.60.51" or RemoteUrl has "39.107.60.51")
| where RemotePort == 80 or RemoteUrl has "/api/software/"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, LocalIP, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2 = "39.107.60.51";
union isfuzzy=true
  (ImWebSession
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DstIpAddr == C2 or Url has C2 or Url has "/api/software/"
    | where HttpMethod == "POST" or isempty(HttpMethod)
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, Url, HttpMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent, HttpRequestBodyBytes, EventVendor, EventProduct),
  (CommonSecurityLog
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(240d)
    | where DestinationIP == C2 or RequestURL has "39.107.60.51/api/software/"
    | where RequestMethod =~ "POST" or isempty(RequestMethod)
    | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname=SourceHostName, SrcUsername=SourceUserName, DstIpAddr=DestinationIP, DstPortNumber=DestinationPort, Url=RequestURL, HttpMethod=RequestMethod, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent=RequestClientApplication, HttpRequestBodyBytes=SentBytes, EventVendor=DeviceVendor, EventProduct=DeviceProduct)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
