Malicious JetBrains plugin folder or JAR present in plugins directory AIInstallation Medium
Hunting query for file-system artefacts of the 15 malicious plugins on developer endpoints — surfaces JAR/folder creations under the JetBrains plugins directory whose name matches one of the 14 disclosed display names or whose plugin ID (org.sm.yms.toolkit, com.json.simple.kit, etc.) appears in path. Helps you find compromised endpoints even after JetBrains' kill-switch has neutered the plugin's execution. Rationale: Anchored on the 14 plugin display names and 14 plugin IDs the article lists verbatim in Table 1. The path predicate \\JetBrains\\...\\plugins\\ narrows scope to the IDE plugins directory which has no legitimate user write activity outside of marketplace installs. Display-name match alone could collide with the legit 'CodeGPT' plugin so we also check plugin IDs which are wholly attacker-controlled and unique.
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1505.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user installing the legitimate 'CodeGPT' Marketplace plugin (distinct plugin ID — verify against the 14 IDs in the article)
  • Developer rebuilding an IDE config from a backup that pre-dates the JetBrains kill-switch
  • Forensic responder copying the malicious plugin JAR to an analysis VM
  • IDE settings sync from a previously-compromised paired developer machine
  • CI/CD pipeline that bakes IDE installations into golden images and tests one of these names
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("\\quarantine\\","\\malware-samples\\","\\forensics\\","\\sandbox\\"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: Confirm the file path is under a real JetBrains plugins directory (not a quarantine/sample folder). Inventory which plugin ID(s) hit — cross-reference Table 1 of the article to identify which malicious plugin. Capture file hash. 2. CONTAIN: Force restart of the JetBrains IDE on the host (triggers JetBrains' remote kill-switch). Delete the offending plugin folder. Treat any AI provider key the user has used (OpenAI, DeepSeek, SiliconFlow) as compromised: rotate immediately and audit provider billing/usage for unauthorized calls. 3. HUNT: Sweep developer fleet for any of the 14 display names or 14 plugin IDs in plugins directories. Pivot on the user's git history for accidentally committed sk- keys. Check 39.107.60.51 connection history per UC1 to identify which keys were actually exfiltrated.

let bad_plugin_ids = dynamic(["org.sm.yms.toolkit","com.json.simple.kit","org.bug.find.tools","org.translate.ai.simple","com.yy.test.ai.simple","com.dev.ai.toolkit","com.json.view.simple","com.my.git.ai.kit","org.check.ai.ds","com.review.tool.code","org.code.assist.dev.tool","com.coder.ai.dpt","com.my.code.tools","ord.cp.code.ai.kit"]);
DeviceFileEvents

| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileRenamed")
| where FolderPath has @"\JetBrains\" and FolderPath has @"\plugins\"
| where FolderPath has_any (bad_display_names) or FileName has_any (bad_display_names) or FolderPath has_any (bad_plugin_ids) or FileName has_any (bad_plugin_ids)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileSize
| order by Timestamp desc

JetBrains IDE plaintext HTTP (port 80) egress to external host AICommand & Control Medium
Behavioural hunt for the defense-evasion technique flagged in the article — the malicious plugins installed a JVM-wide X509TrustManager to suppress TLS warnings, then exfiltrated over plaintext HTTP on port 80 to dodge TLS-inspection telemetry. Legitimate JetBrains IDE traffic is overwhelmingly HTTPS (Marketplace, update channels, license check); a JetBrains IDE making port-80 outbound to a public IP is a strong anomaly signal that catches this campaign and future copycats that retain the plaintext-HTTP exfil pattern with a different IP. Rationale: Article explicitly calls out the TLS warning suppression + plaintext HTTP (port 80) exfil as a deliberate evasion choice: 'while it makes interception trivial for network defenders, it also means the attacker avoided the complexity of managing TLS certificates.' Legitimate JetBrains traffic — Marketplace, updates, license check — is HTTPS, so port-80 JetBrains egress to public IPs is a strong anomaly. Excludes jetbrains.com/intellij.net to suppress the few legitimate HTTP redirects.
ATT&CKT1573 T1071.001 T1562.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Air-gapped/on-prem artifact repo (Nexus, Artifactory) serving Gradle/Maven dependencies over HTTP
  • Internal license server reachable only over HTTP
  • Developer manually pointing the IDE at an HTTP-only test API while debugging
  • Corporate proxy auto-config script forcing HTTP for certain destinations
  • First-launch IDE telemetry that briefly hits an HTTP captive-portal check
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteIP in ("10.","172.16.","172.17.","172.18.","172.19.","172.20.","172.21.","172.22.","172.23.","172.24.","172.25.","172.26.","172.27.","172.28.","172.29.","172.30.","172.31.","192.168.") or RemoteUrl has_any ("artifactory","nexus","jfrog","sonatype"))
Response runbook
1. TRIAGE: For each src→dst pair, resolve the dst IP — is it a known corporate Maven/Nexus/Artifactory server? If yes, allowlist. If unknown / external, treat as suspicious. Pull the IDE log at %APPDATA%\JetBrains\<IDE>\log\idea.log for plugin load entries around the connection time. 2. CONTAIN: If the dst IP matches 39.107.60.51 or any other suspicious external host, follow the UC1 containment workflow (rotate API keys, force IDE restart, block egress). 3. HUNT: Pivot on the dst IP — has any other developer endpoint reached it? Run UC3 (file detection) on the host to see which plugin was installed. Look for any X-Api-Key headers on the dst connection if proxy header logging is on.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","pycharm.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","rubymine64.exe","clion64.exe","goland64.exe","rider64.exe","datagrip64.exe","fleet.exe","studio64.exe","aqua64.exe","rustrover64.exe","dataspell64.exe")
| where RemotePort == 80
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("jetbrains.com","intellij.net","plugins.jetbrains.com"))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp), ConnCount = count(), SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 5) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP
| order by FirstSeen desc
let JBIDEs = dynamic(["idea64.exe","idea.exe","pycharm64.exe","pycharm.exe","webstorm64.exe","phpstorm64.exe","rubymine64.exe","clion64.exe","goland64.exe","rider64.exe","datagrip64.exe","fleet.exe","studio64.exe","aqua64.exe","rustrover64.exe"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)

| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), ConnCount = count(), SampleUrls = make_set(Url, 5) by SrcHostname, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest

| sort - count

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT

| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"

      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

Gravity SMTP WordPress plugin info-disclosure exploit (CVE-2026-4020) AIExploitation High
Hunts unauthenticated GET requests to the vulnerable Gravity SMTP REST endpoint /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data, which returns a JSON System Report containing live SES, Google, Mailjet, Resend and Zoho API credentials when the plugin is <= 2.1.4. Wordfence reports 17M+ blocked attempts against this exact path with a 4M-request spike on June 7, 2026, so a single successful (HTTP 200) response is a credential-compromise event. Rationale: Anchored on the two article-specific IOCs Defiant/Wordfence published: the REST path /wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data and the ?page=gravitysmtp-settings query parameter (the latter distinguishes automated exploit tooling from opportunistic probing). The detection separates Attempts from Successes (HTTP 200) so the SOC can prioritise the small subset where the System Report was actually returned and credentials need rotating. Defender, Datadog standard sources, Falcon EDR and CloudWatch are intentionally empty: this is a server-side web-access-log detection and none of those telemetry layers see inbound WordPress HTTP requests in a default deployment. No external corroboration searched — the Bleeping Computer article cites the primary Wordfence/Defiant advisory and the IOC strings are unambiguous.
ATT&CKT1190 T1552.001 T1589.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised external vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Tenable.io, Burp Suite) probing the endpoint within an approved scope — typically high attempts, no Successes
  • Wordfence / WPScan post-patch verification scans hitting every known-vulnerable plugin path
  • Internal blue/purple team patch-validation hitting the path from a corporate jump host or VPN egress IP
  • SRE / support engineers pulling the System Report through the admin UI for troubleshooting — originates from an authenticated admin session via the wp-admin POST path, not direct GET to the REST endpoint
  • Mass-Internet scanners (Censys, Shodan, ShadowServer) opportunistically probing /wp-json/* — usually distinguishable by hitting many other plugins' REST routes in the same window
Suppression filter
| where SrcIpAddr !in (dynamic(["<authorised-scanner-IP>", "<internal-jumphost-IP>"]))
| where HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Wordfence" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "WPScan" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Nessus" and HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent !has "Qualys"
Response runbook
1) Triage — confirm `Successes` > 0 for the SrcIpAddr; a single 200 means the JSON System Report (SES/Google/Mailjet/Resend/Zoho API keys, DB table names, plugin inventory, PHP env) was exfiltrated. Pull the response size from WAF/proxy logs to verify a real payload (typically several KB). Cross-reference the target site's installed Gravity SMTP version against 2.1.5. 2) Contain — immediately upgrade Gravity SMTP to >= 2.1.5 on every affected site, then rotate every credential the plugin had configured: AWS SES access-key pairs, Google service-account tokens / OAuth refresh tokens, Mailjet / Resend / Zoho API keys, and any plain-SMTP passwords. Block the SrcIpAddr at the WAF/CDN and add to the org IP blocklist; pull all WP REST endpoints in the same time window to catch lateral plugin probing. 3) Hunt — query AWS CloudTrail SES SendEmail / SendRawEmail / SendBulkTemplatedEmail and Google Workspace mailflow audit logs for unauthorised sends in the 48h after the first successful exfil;
let lookback = 7d;
// ASIM web-session view normalises IIS, Apache, Nginx, F5, Azure App Gateway and most WAFs.
// If ASIM parsers are not enabled, swap ImWebSession for W3CIISLog / AzureDiagnostics / CommonSecurityLog.
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Url has "/wp-json/gravitysmtp/v1/tests/mock-data"
| extend HasSettingsParam = Url has "page=gravitysmtp-settings"
| extend StatusCode = coalesce(HttpResponseCode, HttpStatusCode)
| summarize
    Attempts    = count(),
    Successes   = countif(StatusCode == 200),                // 200 = System Report exfiltrated
    Blocked     = countif(StatusCode between (400 .. 599)),
    FirstSeen   = min(TimeGenerated),
    LastSeen    = max(TimeGenerated),
    TargetSites = dcount(DstHostname),
    SitesList   = make_set(DstHostname, 20),
    SampleUA    = any(HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent),
    SampleUrl   = any(Url)
    by SrcIpAddr, HasSettingsParam
| extend Severity = case(Successes > 0, "High",
                         HasSettingsParam and Attempts >= 5, "Medium",
                         "Low")
| order by Successes desc, Attempts desc

Gentlemen RaaS / GentleKiller BYOVD driver file drop (.sys IOC set) AIInstallation High
Detects on-disk staging of any of the 13 vulnerable/malicious drivers abused by GentleKiller, HexKiller, ThrottleBlood, and HavocKiller (eb.sys, nseckrnl.sys, GameDriverX64.sys, stpm_old/new.sys, dmx.sys, 360netmon_wfp.sys, IMFForceDelete.sys, PoisonX.sys, googleApiUtil64.sys, ThrottleBlood.sys, havoc.sys, hrwfpdrv.sys). Strings are attacker-specific filenames so any write outside an authoritative vendor install path is a strong BYOVD precursor. Rationale: Driver filenames are reproduced verbatim from the article driver-table (eb.sys/nseckrnl.sys/GameDriverX64.sys/stpm_old|new.sys/dmx.sys/360netmon_wfp.sys/IMFForceDelete.sys/PoisonX.sys/googleApiUtil64.sys/ThrottleBlood.sys/havoc.sys) and corroborated by ESET WeLiveSecurity and Huntress (hrwfpdrv.sys + PoisonX.sys co-drop). None of these names match any legitimate vendor install package, so any file-write outside C:\Windows\System32\drivers from a vendor installer is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.huntress.com/blog/encase-byovd-edr-killer • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://threatlabsnews.xcitium.com/blog/reverse-engineering-a-0-day-poisonx-byovd-driver-bypasses-crowdstrike-edr/
ATT&CKT1068 T1014 T1562.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security researcher staging captured samples to a malware lab share
  • EDR/AV vendor pulling a sample to a sandboxed analysis VM (InitiatingProcess = sandbox controller)
  • Threat-hunting team importing IOCs into a forensics workstation
  • Backup-restore operation rehydrating an old quarantine folder containing one of the .sys files
  • Penetration test using a public BYOVD repo (e.g. GitHub BlackSnufkin/BYOVD) - should be allow-listed by host tag
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\msiexec.exe", @"\Program Files\") and InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Kaspersky","FACEIT","Riot Games","Qihoo 360","Huawei","Safetica","Zemana","IObit"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull SHA256 of the dropped .sys and the InitiatingProcess, check against ESET/Huntress IOCs and VT - simultaneously isolate the device from the network (Defender 'Isolate Device'). 2) Contain: kill the InitiatingProcess tree, delete the driver file, and block the SHA256 + InitiatingProcess hash at the EDR; check if a kernel service was created (see UC2) - if yes, mark service Disabled and reboot in safe mode. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet, search for the same hash chain on other endpoints in last 30 days, and check for BeyondTrust Remote Support / RMM session preceding the drop (per Huntress, that was the access vector in one Gentlemen intrusion).

BYOVD kernel-driver service registration via Services\ImagePath AIInstallation High
Detects registry writes that register one of the Gentlemen-arsenal .sys drivers as a Windows kernel service (Services\\<name>\\ImagePath), the load step that follows the file drop in UC1. The combined chain (drop -> service register -> NtLoadDriver) is the canonical BYOVD attack flow. Rationale: Per ESET, each GentleKiller variant abuses a different vulnerable driver and registers it as a kernel service - the article lists the eight first-party drivers and three third-party drivers verbatim. Catching ImagePath references to these exact filenames in any Services\\<name> key is high-fidelity because legitimate kernel-mode software for these products installs to vendor-specific service names (e.g. klhk for Kaspersky) under InProgramFiles paths, not arbitrary user-named services. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1547.006 T1068
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Kaspersky/FACEIT/Valorant install on a corporate gaming-test or red-team box (eb.sys/nseckrnl.sys/GameDriverX64.sys may appear in legit service path)
  • Vendor reinstall after an uninstall left an orphaned service key
  • MDM agent re-deploying endpoint protection that bundles one of the impersonated drivers
  • Forensic imaging tool registering driver service during live-response (e.g. KAPE / X-Ways)
  • Penetration test or BYOVD research lab
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryValueData has_any (@"C:\Program Files\Kaspersky Lab\", @"C:\Program Files (x86)\FACEIT\", @"C:\Riot Games\VALORANT\", @"C:\Program Files\Qihoo\", @"C:\Program Files\Huawei\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the ImagePath and confirm the driver file is the dropped one from UC1 (cross-ref SHA256); check parent of InitiatingProcess for an RMM or remote-session indicator (BeyondTrust, AnyDesk, ScreenConnect). 2) Contain: isolate the host, run 'sc stop <servicename>' and 'sc delete <servicename>', delete the .sys file, and quarantine the dropper hash globally. 3) Hunt: query for the same ServiceName across the fleet, search Windows Event 7045 (System log) for the same image path in last 90 days, and look for follow-on Process Access / OpenProcessApiCall events targeting EDR processes (see UC3).
let GentlemenDrivers = dynamic(["eb.sys","nseckrnl.sys","GameDriverX64.sys","stpm_old.sys","stpm_new.sys","dmx.sys","360netmon_wfp.sys","IMFForceDelete.sys","PoisonX.sys","googleApiUtil64.sys","ThrottleBlood.sys","havoc.sys","hrwfpdrv.sys"]);

| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
| where RegistryKey has @"\System\CurrentControlSet\Services\"
| where RegistryValueName =~ "ImagePath"
| where RegistryValueData has_any (GentlemenDrivers)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,

Mass EDR/security-process tampering (GentleKiller 400-process kill list) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects a single initiating process accessing or terminating multiple distinct security-vendor processes within a short window - the behavioural signature of GentleKiller iterating its 400-process / 48-product target list after BYOVD driver load. Independent of which driver was used, this catches the kill stage even when the driver name is obfuscated. Rationale: Article states GentleKiller iterates through 400 processes across 48 distinct security products; ESET write-up enumerates the impersonated vendors (Kaspersky/CrowdStrike/Safetica/Zemana/Qihoo 360/IObit/Huawei). The behavioural signature - one process touching N distinct security-vendor binaries within a 5-minute window - is what every GentleKiller variant emits regardless of which BYOVD driver carried it. dcount>=5 chosen as a conservative threshold (P99 in any baseline is 1-2 legitimate AV-vs-AV touches on uninstall). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/ • https://threatlabsnews.xcitium.com/blog/reverse-engineering-a-0-day-poisonx-byovd-driver-bypasses-crowdstrike-edr/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint protection migration where IT runs a vendor-supplied uninstaller that legitimately stops competing AV products
  • MDM/RMM 'security cleanup' script that uses taskkill or sc stop on a known set of competing AVs
  • Sysinternals PsKill / Process Explorer kill operation by a sysadmin doing forensic triage
  • Antivirus vendor's own self-test/self-protection check accessing peer-vendor binaries to enumerate co-existence
  • Backup software (Veeam/Acronis) excluding AV processes via OpenProcess for snapshot quiescence
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","uninstall.exe","msiexec.exe","PsKill.exe","PsKill64.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Windows\Installer\")) | where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Veeam","Acronis","Sysinternals","Microsoft Corporation"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessSHA256 and the full Targets list - confirm the initiator is not a known IT cleanup tool; check for the prior driver-drop chain (UC1) or service registration (UC2) within the last 24h on the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host immediately - if 5+ EDR processes were touched, assume defenses are blind; force an out-of-band reimage candidate flag and disable the user's domain account. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 to find every host that ran the dropper, look for shadow-copy deletion / ransomware notes (post-EDR-kill stage), and pull any BeyondTrust Remote Support sessions or Bomgar/Bomgar-related processes in the same logon session.

let SecVendorProcs = dynamic(["MsMpEng.exe","MsSense.exe","NisSrv.exe","SecurityHealthService.exe","CSFalconService.exe","CSFalconContainer.exe","SentinelAgent.exe","SentinelHelperService.exe","SentinelStaticEngine.exe","ekrn.exe","egui.exe","avp.exe","avpui.exe","kavfs.exe","klnagent.exe","mfemms.exe","mfevtps.exe","TaniumClient.exe","ir_agent.exe","Rapid7Agent.exe","amsvc.exe","cyserver.exe","cytray.exe","CarbonBlackProtect.exe","TmListen.exe","TMBMSRV.exe","NTRTScan.exe","Bdagent.exe","vsserv.exe","fortiedr.exe","forticlient.exe","SophosAgent.exe","SAVService.exe","HMPAlert.exe","WRSA.exe","xagt.exe","PccNTMon.exe"]);

OxideHarvest credential stealer - single process scraping multiple browser stores AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the Rust-based OxideHarvest (aka buildx641) stealer behaviour: one process opens Login Data / cookies / logins.json across 3+ of the 13 browsers the article names (Chrome, Edge, Torch, Comodo, Epic Privacy, Vivaldi, Brave, Opera, OperaGX, Firefox, Waterfox, BlackHawk, IceCat) within a tight window. The breadth of profile paths touched - well beyond what any single browser would self-access - is the high-fidelity signal. Rationale: Article names the exact 13 browsers OxideHarvest (buildx641) targets verbatim: Chrome, Edge, Torch, Comodo, Epic Privacy Browser, Vivaldi, Brave, Opera, OperaGX, Firefox, Waterfox, BlackHawk, IceCat. A real user uses 1-2 browsers; a non-browser process touching the Login Data / logins.json / key4.db across three of these in a 10-minute window is OxideHarvest's exact scan pattern. The exclusion of the browser binaries themselves prevents the obvious FP (the browsers reading their own credential stores). Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Browser-data migration utility (e.g. Microsoft Edge import-from-Chrome wizard) reading peer-browser profiles
  • Password manager (1Password, Bitwarden, KeePass) import wizard scanning all installed browsers
  • Endpoint DLP product scanning user-data directories for compliance
  • Backup product (e.g. CrashPlan, OneDrive Known Folder Move) opening profile files for incremental backup
  • Sysadmin running BrowserDownloadsView / NirSoft credential audit tools on a triage workstation
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any ("Microsoft Corporation","Mozilla","Google LLC","1Password","AgileBits","Bitwarden","KeePass") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessSHA256 / InitiatingProcessFolderPath - if path is under \Users\Public, \AppData\Local\Temp, or \ProgramData and SHA is not in baseline, treat as confirmed OxideHarvest. Check network egress from same host in the same window for a Rust-runtime user-agent or unfamiliar HTTPS destination. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force user password reset for every browser-saved credential the user manages, revoke any active SSO sessions, and rotate any service-account credentials cached in those stores. 3) Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet for prior executions, look for follow-on GentleKiller / BYOVD driver activity (UC1/UC2) on the same host (OxideHarvest typically precedes the ransomware payload), and review SSO/AAD sign-in logs for impossible-travel after the harvest time.
let BrowserProfiles = dynamic([@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\", @"\Vivaldi\User Data\", @"\Opera Software\Opera Stable\", @"\Opera Software\Opera GX Stable\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\", @"\Waterfox\Profiles\", @"\Torch\User Data\", @"\Comodo\Dragon\User Data\", @"\Epic Privacy Browser\User Data\", @"\NETGATE Technologies\BlackHawk Web Browser\", @"\IceCat\Profiles\"]);
let CredFiles = dynamic(["Login Data","Login Data For Account","logins.json","key4.db","key3.db","cookies.sqlite","Cookies","Web Data"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (CredFiles)
| where FolderPath has_any (BrowserProfiles)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
      and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
      and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| extend BrowserRoot = extract(@"(\\(?:Google\\Chrome|Microsoft\\Edge|BraveSoftware\\Brave-Browser|Vivaldi|Opera Software\\Opera Stable|Opera Software\\Opera GX Stable|Mozilla\\Firefox|Waterfox|Torch|Comodo\\Dragon|Epic Privacy Browser|NETGATE Technologies\\BlackHawk Web Browser|IceCat))", 1, FolderPath)
| summarize DistinctBrowsers = dcount(BrowserRoot),
            BrowsersTouched = make_set(BrowserRoot, 20),

Security-vendor-impersonating binary (Enigma/Themida packed) executing from non-vendor path AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for the GentleKiller impersonation layer: a binary whose VersionInfo CompanyName / ProductName / Icon mimics a real security vendor (Kaspersky, ESET, Trend Micro, Bitdefender, Sophos, Qihoo 360, Huawei, Safetica, Zemana, IObit, etc.) but executes from a user/temp/programdata path, optionally with Enigma or Themida packer artifacts visible. Catches the dropper itself before BYOVD driver registration. Rationale: Article states GentleKiller variants are 'standardized through a shared defense-evasion layer, impersonating predominantly security vendors using fake version information, and copied legitimate certificates and icons' and ESET WeLiveSecurity enumerates the impersonated vendors. Real security-vendor binaries never execute from \Users\, \Temp\, or \ProgramData\; they live under \Program Files\<vendor>\. The combination of (vendor CompanyName) AND (non-vendor path) is the exact masquerading signature. Cross-checked against: • https://www.welivesecurity.com/en/eset-research/killing-me-gently-inside-gentlemens-edr-killer-framework/ • https://www.bleepingcomputer.com/news/security/gentlemen-ransomware-uses-multiple-edr-killers-to-disable-defenses/
ATT&CKT1036.001 T1036.005 T1027.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Vendor installer extracting transient executable copies to \Users\<user>\AppData\Local\Temp during install
  • Sysinternals or Microsoft Sysmon binary executed from a user Tools folder (Microsoft Corporation CompanyName)
  • Endpoint protection update/redistribution staged from a shared \ProgramData\<vendor>\Update\ path
  • Driver/agent removal tools (TrendMicroDiagnosticToolkit, ESETUninstaller, KAVRemover) run from Desktop or Downloads
  • Security researcher analysing a vendor sample on a triage VM
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("msiexec.exe","setup.exe","installer.exe","vssadmin.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith @"C:\Windows\") | where ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName !endswith "Removal Tool.exe" and ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName !endswith "Uninstaller.exe"
Response runbook
1) Triage: detonate the SHA256 in a sandbox, check for Enigma/Themida packer indicators (high-entropy section, anti-debug imports, suspicious section names like .enigma1/.themida); pivot on the same hash across the fleet. 2) Contain: if confirmed packed-and-impersonating, block hash at EDR globally, isolate the originating host, and check whether the binary's parent process was a remote-access tool (BeyondTrust / AnyDesk / ScreenConnect). 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1/UC2 (driver drop + service registration) and UC3 (mass EDR kill) for the same DeviceName in the prior 24h window; if any match, treat as full GentleKiller deployment and assume credential exposure.
let SecVendors = dynamic(["Kaspersky","ESET","Bitdefender","Trend Micro","Sophos","CrowdStrike","SentinelOne","Symantec","NortonLifeLock","McAfee","Microsoft Corporation","Qihoo 360","Huawei","Safetica","Zemana","IObit","Malwarebytes","Avast","AVG Technologies","Cylance","Carbon Black","Tanium","Rapid7","Cybereason","FireEye"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName)
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has_any (SecVendors)
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\PerfLogs\", @"\Windows\Temp\")
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
      and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
      and FolderPath !contains @"\WindowsApps\"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
          ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, ProcessVersionInfoProductName,
          ProcessVersionInfoOriginalFileName, ProcessVersionInfoFileDescription,
          ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let SecVendors = dynamic(["Kaspersky","ESET","Bitdefender","Trend Micro","Sophos","CrowdStrike","SentinelOne","Symantec","McAfee","Microsoft Corporation","Qihoo 360","Huawei","Safetica","Zemana","IObit","Malwarebytes","Avast","Cylance","Carbon Black","Tanium","Rapid7","Cybereason","FireEye"]);
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where isnotempty(ActingProcessFileCompany)
| where ActingProcessFileCompany has_any (SecVendors)
| where ActingProcessName has_any (@"\Users\", @"\AppData\", @"\Temp\", @"\Public\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\PerfLogs\")
| where ActingProcessName !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
      and ActingProcessName !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          ActingProcessFileCompany, ActingProcessFileProduct,
          ActingProcessFileOriginalName, ActingProcessFileDescription,
          ActingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\Users\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\Public\\* OR *\\ProgramData\\* OR *\\PerfLogs\\*) -@Image:(*\\Program Files\\* OR *\\Program Files (x86)\\*) @Company:(*Kaspersky* OR *ESET* OR *Bitdefender* OR *"Trend Micro"* OR *Sophos* OR *CrowdStrike* OR *SentinelOne* OR *Symantec* OR *McAfee* OR *"Qihoo 360"* OR *Huawei* OR *Safetica* OR *Zemana* OR *IObit* OR *Malwarebytes*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(Users|AppData|Temp|Public|ProgramData|PerfLogs)\\/i
| !ImageFileName=/^[A-Z]:\\Program Files( \(x86\))?\\/i
| CompanyName=/(Kaspersky|ESET|Bitdefender|Trend Micro|Sophos|CrowdStrike|SentinelOne|Symantec|McAfee|Qihoo 360|Huawei|Safetica|Zemana|IObit|Malwarebytes|Microsoft Corporation)/i

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s) Reconnaissance High
Match vulnerability scanner output to the CVE(s) named in the article.
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-26125")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
          VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Vulnerabilities
    where Vulnerabilities.signature IN ("CVE-2025-26125")
    by Vulnerabilities.dest, Vulnerabilities.signature, Vulnerabilities.severity, Vulnerabilities.cve
| `drop_dm_object_name(Vulnerabilities)`
| sort - severity
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_psexec:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\wmic.exe'
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '/node:'
    condition: selection_psexec or selection_wmic_remote
falsepositives:
    - Sysadmins running approved remote-management tooling — wrap with
      a known-admin-host watchlist
level: high

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")

| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc

``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AutoJack Attack Lets One Web Page Hijack AI Agent for Host Code Execution

The Hacker News
2026-06-19 10 use cases 4 techniques 7 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft researchers have detailed an exploit chain, named&nbsp;AutoJack, that turns an AI browsing agent into a delivery vehicle for remote code execution. Steer the agent to load an attacker's web page, and that page's JavaScript can reach a privileged local service on the same machine and spawn a process on the host. No credentials, no sign-in screen, and no further user interaction once

AutoGen Studio Python process spawns shell or calc.exe (AutoJack MCP RCE outcome) AIExploitation High
Detects the AutoJack chain's terminal effect: an unauthenticated WebSocket command landing on AutoGen Studio's MCP endpoint results in the Python interpreter hosting autogenstudio spawning an arbitrary executable. The PoC pops calc.exe; in the wild any shell, scripting host, or LOLBin child of a python process whose command line references the autogenstudio module is high-fidelity. Rationale: Anchors on the article's two unique strings: parent process is the Python interpreter and the parent command line contains 'autogenstudio' (the module entrypoint Microsoft shipped). Child set models the PoC (calc.exe) plus the realistic post-RCE attacker pivots an unauthenticated MCP command would launch. Cross-checked against the maintainers' fix at github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362 (commit b047730). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362
ATT&CKT1203 T1059.001 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AutoGen Studio sample notebooks/tutorials that legitimately spawn calc.exe as a 'hello world' tool demo (Microsoft's own quickstart uses this).
  • Developers running AutoGen Studio agents whose registered tools are literally cmd.exe or powershell.exe sub-process invocations (intended tool-use).
  • CI/integration tests that exercise the autogenstudio package and shell out to certutil/curl for fixture downloads.
  • Conda/venv activation wrappers where python.exe spawns cmd.exe to set environment before the real agent runs.
Suppression filter
and not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\autogen\\samples\\","\\autogen\\notebook","\\autogenstudio\\tests\\","pytest","unittest") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\autogen\\samples\\","\\autogenstudio\\tests\\","pytest","-m unittest"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the full process tree on the host — confirm the python.exe parent's command line and capture the child process command line. Run `pip show autogenstudio` (or inspect site-packages/_version.py) to confirm whether the vulnerable 0.4.3.dev1/dev2 is installed. Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the python PID in the 60s preceding the spawn — an inbound localhost WebSocket on the autogenstudio port plus an outbound fetch of an untrusted URL by a browsing-agent process is the AutoJack signature. 2. Contain: stop the autogenstudio process, isolate the host, and block any external URL the agent fetched in the last hour at the proxy. 3. Hunt: pivot on DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory for every host with autogenstudio installed; rerun the parent/child query across that fleet for the last 30 days; check DeviceRegistryEvents and scheduled tasks created under the autogenstudio python context for persistence.

| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","calc.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","wsl.exe")

Vulnerable AutoGen Studio pre-release installed via pip (autogenstudio 0.4.3.dev1/dev2) AIWeaponization High
Detects installation of the two AutoJack-vulnerable AutoGen Studio pre-release builds Microsoft confirmed shipped to PyPI: 0.4.3.dev1 and 0.4.3.dev2. The vulnerable MCP WebSocket handler exists only in those builds; neither has been yanked and no patched PyPI build exists. Catches both explicit version pinning and the `--pre autogenstudio` form that resolves to a dev build. Rationale: Anchors on the two PyPI version strings Microsoft's PSIRT confirmed contain the vulnerable handler (0.4.3.dev1, 0.4.3.dev2) plus the only other path to those builds (--pre flag, which resolves to the highest pre-release). The article is explicit that the stable 0.4.2.2 is NOT vulnerable, so we don't false-positive on plain installs. Cross-checked against PR #7362 in the autogen repo which contains the fix that has not yet shipped to PyPI. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • AutoGen contributors / Microsoft Research engineers intentionally pulling the dev build to test the patched main branch.
  • AI engineering team running `pip install --pre autogenstudio` in a sandboxed venv to evaluate new agent features.
  • CI pipelines that install --pre to track upstream for compatibility testing.
  • Security researchers reproducing AutoJack in a lab — expected and benign on the research bench, alert on production hosts.
Suppression filter
and not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\venv\\","\\.venv\\","\\sandbox\\","\\research\\") or DeviceName startswith "RESEARCH-" or DeviceName startswith "LAB-")
Response runbook
1. Triage: identify the host and user; run `pip show autogenstudio` to confirm installed version; check whether the host also runs a browsing/code-execution agent that shares the same localhost (the chain prerequisite). 2. Contain: uninstall the dev build (`pip uninstall autogenstudio`) and install from GitHub main at or after commit b047730 (the article notes no fixed PyPI build yet exists). If immediate upgrade isn't possible, run AutoGen Studio under a low-privilege account in an isolated container/VM separate from any browsing agent. 3. Hunt: pivot to UC1's parent/child query against this host for the 30 days preceding install and ongoing; check DeviceNetworkEvents for inbound 127.0.0.1 WebSocket connections to the python listener; review autogenstudio config for the `auth_mode` setting that the article calls out as a misleading control.
let PipInstalls = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where (FileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip install"))
    | where ProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("0.4.3.dev1","0.4.3.dev2","==0.4.3.dev","--pre");
let PackageDrops = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
    | where FolderPath has @"\site-packages\autogenstudio"
    | where FileName in~ ("version.py","_version.py","__init__.py","METADATA","PKG-INFO")
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("pip.exe","pip3.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe");
PipInstalls
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, Source="pip-cmdline"
| union (PackageDrops | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source="site-packages-write")
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetProcessName has_any ("pip.exe","pip3.exe") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("pip install","-m pip install")
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
| where TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("0.4.3.dev1","0.4.3.dev2","==0.4.3.dev","--pre")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetProcessName, TargetProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Persistence written by AutoGen Studio Python process (Run keys / scheduled tasks) AIInstallation High
Detects post-exploitation persistence registered by the AutoGen Studio Python process — the AutoJack RCE gives an attacker arbitrary command execution under the developer's account, and the natural next step is a Run-key or scheduled-task drop to survive an agent restart. Article-specific because we anchor on the parent being the autogenstudio python interpreter, not a generic LOLBin. Rationale: Anchors on the same two strings as UC1 (python interpreter + 'autogenstudio' in parent command line) but pivots to registry/scheduled-task telemetry. The AutoJack RCE runs under the developer's account so persistence keys/tasks would inherit that same identity — and the parent process chain unambiguously names autogenstudio. Cross-checked against PR #7362 fix scope (the fix only blocks the unauth path, not post-exploit persistence — so this detection remains valuable even on patched builds). Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/microsoft/autogen/pull/7362
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1053.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer installing AutoGen Studio as a tray/auto-start app and intentionally adding a Run key for it at install time.
  • AutoGen agents whose registered toolset legitimately uses schtasks.exe to schedule periodic jobs (rare, but possible for automation-focused agents).
  • AutoGen Studio installer/uninstaller writing Uninstall keys (different hive path, but worth excluding if the rule is broadened).
  • Python-packaged AutoGen Studio service installer (`autogenstudio install-service`) registering a scheduled task on first run.
Suppression filter
and not (RegistryValueData has_any ("\\autogenstudio\\","AutoGen Studio.exe","autogenstudio-tray") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("install-service","--register-autostart","setup.py install"))
Response runbook
1. Triage: pull the persistence artifact (registry key + value, or scheduled-task XML). Compare RegistryValueData / task action against what AutoGen Studio's official installer writes — anything that points to a non-autogenstudio binary, encoded command, or temp-path script is the RCE outcome. 2. Contain: delete the persistence entry, terminate the autogenstudio python process, and isolate the host. Preserve the registry hive / task XML for forensics. 3. Hunt: rerun UC1 (parent/child shell spawn) for the 24h before the persistence write to identify the initial RCE event; pull DeviceNetworkEvents for the autogenstudio python PID to identify the attacker URL the browsing agent loaded; check every host with autogenstudio installed for the same persistence pattern over the last 30 days.
let RegistryPersistence = DeviceRegistryEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
    | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
    | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Explorer\Shell Folders\Startup", @"\Image File Execution Options")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
              RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Persistence="registry";
let TaskCreates = DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe","python3.11.exe","python3.12.exe")
    | where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
    | where FileName in~ ("schtasks.exe","at.exe") or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("schtasks /create","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
              RegistryKey="", RegistryValueName="", RegistryValueData=ProcessCommandLine,
              InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Persistence="scheduled-task";
RegistryPersistence
| union TaskCreates
| order by Timestamp desc
let RegPers = ImRegistryEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ActingProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe")
    | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
    | where RegistryKey has_any (@"\CurrentVersion\Run", @"\CurrentVersion\RunOnce", @"\Explorer\Shell Folders\Startup", @"\Image File Execution Options")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessCommandLine, Persistence="registry";
let TaskPers = ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where ParentProcessName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","python3.exe")
    | where ParentProcessCommandLine has "autogenstudio"
    | where TargetProcessName has_any ("schtasks.exe","at.exe") or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("schtasks /create","Register-ScheduledTask","New-ScheduledTask")
    | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, RegistryKey="", RegistryValue="", RegistryValueData=TargetProcessCommandLine, ActingProcessCommandLine=ParentProcessCommandLine, Persistence="scheduled-task";
RegPers
| union TaskPers
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2026-26030", "CVE-2026-25592")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`

| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
